rationale: Available literature from OMIM entry #618443 and the seminal discovery cohort by Platzer et al. (2019) confirms that epileptic seizures are not considered a prominent or core manifestation of MAPK8IP3-related neurodevelopmental disorder (NEDBA), with Platzer et al. noting 'very limited evidence that seizures are truly part of the phenotypic spectrum'. Recent familial reports (such as Yi et al., 2026, describing an inherited loss-of-function splice-site variant) demonstrate milder neurodevelopmental manifestations devoid of seizures, supporting the observation that seizures occur inconsistently and are absent in loss-of-function pedigrees. While individual cases with oligogenic modifiers (e.g., Krenn et al., 2025) or isolated missense series have noted epilepsy, overall seizure frequency across molecularly confirmed cohorts remains low (frequently cited as <25% in aggregate cohorts), confirming its classification as a secondary, variable phenotype rather than a core clinical diagnostic criterion.

evidence.text: Platzer et al. evaluated 13 unrelated individuals with de novo variants in MAPK8IP3 and observed that there is very limited evidence that seizures are truly part of the phenotypic spectrum of the disorder.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact penetrance of electroencephalographic (EEG) epileptiform discharges versus clinical seizures when stratified strictly by MAPK8IP3 variant class (recurrent missense in kinesin/cargo-binding domains vs loss-of-function truncations)?
new_directions.rationale: Discrepancies in clinical seizure reporting may stem from under-recognized subclinical EEG abnormalities or domain-specific gain-of-function/dominant-negative mechanisms versus haploinsufficiency.

new_directions.question_text: Does oligogenic burden from other neuronal transport or excitability genes modulate seizure emergence in individuals with loss-of-function MAPK8IP3 variants?
new_directions.rationale: Single-gene truncations in MAPK8IP3 often show mild developmental phenotypes without seizures, whereas patients presenting with epilepsy (e.g., Krenn et al., 2025) carry secondary truncating variants in genes such as ADAM23 or TNRC6A.
